prime.problem: "Passes" needs a precise rule. Bit-exact float comparison fails correct code, a flat time limit either fails every correct solution on 764 tests or waves slow ones through, and HumanEval's 3 seconds per whole suite was built for 9.6 tests.
prime.fits: Differential testing compares f(x) with gt(x). This card is the rule for what counts as equal, and how long f may take, once there are about 764 inputs per task.
prime.goal: Compute the timeout for any ground-truth time, explain why each of the three rules exists, and say what the timeout makes pass@k measure besides correctness.

attend: Why is a per-suite time limit unworkable once each task has hundreds of tests?
At what ground-truth time does the 4× term take over from the 200 ms floor, and which one do most small Python functions get?
Why does bit-exact float comparison produce false positives, not caught bugs?
What does the 4× rule turn into a failure that a generous limit would pass?
Why does measuring tgt on the evaluation machine make results hardware-dependent?

must: Suite-level budget (3 s) was sized for about 10 tests → 764 tests at even 200 ms each need 152.8 s → a per-suite limit would fail every correct solution → the limit moves to each test

Limit scales with the reference's own time on that input (4 × tgt) → slow solutions fail on heavy inputs → pass@k on HumanEval+ also measures efficiency → matching the 3 performance defects found in the ground truths
Fast tests have noisy timings → 4 × a few ms would flag noise as failure → a 200 ms floor absorbs it → below tgt = 50 ms the floor binds, which is where most tasks sit
Floats differ in the last bits when arithmetic is reordered → exact comparison would fail correct code → a tolerance (annotated, else 1e−6) accepts them → only the degree of slack is a design choice
elevated: tgt is measured on the evaluating machine → a solution near 4× can pass on one box and time out on another → results can be flaky, and the paper doesn't report its hardware

compress.prompt: From memory, state the three parts of EvalPlus's verdict (equality, floats, time), give the timeout formula, and explain in one sentence each why it isn't simpler.
checklist: exact matching against the ground truth's return value
floats within the annotated tolerance or 1e−6
per-test because 764 tests can't share 3 s
the floor absorbs timing noise; the 4× term catches genuinely slow code

retrieve.q: Explain why HumanEval+ pass rates partly measure efficiency, not only functional correctness.
answer: each test fails if it runs longer than max(200 ms, 4 × tgt)
a correct but asymptotically slow solution times out on heavy inputs
so "passes" means correct and no more than about 4× slower than the reference

retrieve.q: Compute the timeout for tgt = 10 ms, 50 ms, 75 ms and 1 s, and say which term binds each time.
Why not simply give every test a generous 10 s? What do you gain and what do you lose?
answer: gain: no flaky timeouts, hardware matters less
lose: performance bugs pass, like the 3 inefficient ground truths
and one task's worst case could take 764 × 10 s, so evaluation gets far slower

compare.q: The Codex paper's sandbox and this oracle both sit around executing untrusted code. What is each one protecting against, and how does each fail?
answer: sandbox: generated code harming the host or network
oracle and timeout: wrong verdicts (float noise, slow code, hangs)
sandbox fails if isolation leaks; the oracle fails on flaky timing or ambiguous output formats
you need both: one keeps you safe, the other keeps the score honest

compare.q: Differential testing says "compare with the ground truth"; the oracle says how. Which verdicts would change if you swapped the oracle for bit-exact, untimed comparison?
answer: correct float code with reordered sums would fail
slow or hanging code would eventually pass (or never finish)
the comparison principle stays; only false positives and missed performance bugs change

predict.q: A task's ground truth runs in 30 ms on the evaluation machine. A sample is correct but 5× slower on every input. Commit: does it pass? What if the ground truth took 120 ms?
predict.answer: At 30 ms the sample takes 150 ms against a 200 ms limit: it passes, because the floor gives 6.7× slack. At 120 ms it takes 600 ms against 480 ms: it fails. The same relative slowness passes on fast tasks and fails on heavy ones, so the 4× rule only really bites where the reference is above 50 ms.

apply.task: Check float tolerance and time in Python. (1) Compute 0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3, and say whether exact comparison and a 1e−6 absolute tolerance accept 0.1 + 0.2 as 0.3. (2) Write timeout(tgt_ms) and find the largest slowdown factor a correct solution can have and still pass, for tgt = 5, 30, 50, 120 ms. (3) One task has 764 tests with tgt = 10 ms each: what is the worst-case total time budget, and how does it compare with HumanEval's 3 s?
apply.done: (1) The difference is about 5.55e−17: exact comparison rejects, the tolerance accepts. (2) Slack is 40×, 6.7×, 4× and 4×. (3) 764 × 200 ms = 152.8 s, about 51 times HumanEval's 3 s.
apply.hint: Slack = timeout / tgt. For tgt ≤ 50 ms the timeout is 200 ms.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 30 ms case or the 120 ms case?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the floor exists at all?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: timeout → performance requirement, or performance requirement → lower pass@k?
Would you call a 5×-slower correct solution wrong? Could you defend the paper's choice?
What will you look for in the leave-one-out card: how the reduced suite avoids judging a model with its own mistakes?
